rows.title: Policy
rows.read: Almost every major central bank is leaning toward raising rates because high oil keeps inflation up. A sharp fall in US bond yields today did not shake bets on a December Federal Reserve hike. Switzerland is the odd one out, where a cut is still possible.

rows.title: Growth
rows.read: The US jobs market is still strong, with layoffs near their lowest in decades. Elsewhere growth is softening at the edges: euro-area households are gloomier, UK factory orders fell and Canadian home prices slipped. None of it has changed central bank plans yet.

rows.title: Inflation
rows.read: Inflation is running hot almost everywhere because of energy, which is why so many central banks lean toward hikes. Canada's factory and raw material prices jumped far more than expected, a sign more inflation is on the way there. Japan's inflation figures tonight matter most for the yen.
rows.figure: Canada IPPI +2.0% m/m (0.7% fc), RMPI +4.8% m/m (0.1% fc); UK CPI Sep 3.5%; NZ Q3 CPI 3.7%; Japan core CPI fc 2.1%, 6:30 PM CT

rows.title: Risk
rows.read: Investors turned nervous: tech shares fell sharply on doubts about AI spending, and reports of planned strikes on Iran added to the worry. Money went into US government bonds and the yen, while the New Zealand dollar fell most. Gold kept sliding instead of acting as a shelter.

rows.title: Terms of trade
rows.read: Oil is at its highest since May on the risk of renewed strikes on Iran. That helps exporters like Canada and hurts big energy importers like Japan and the euro area.

rows.title: Positioning
rows.read: Hedge funds are betting most heavily against the Canadian dollar, even as a Bank of Canada hike looks likely, which leaves those bets exposed if the loonie keeps rising. They also bet against the kiwi and the euro. In the yen and the Aussie, hedge funds and long-term investors take opposite sides.

rows.title: Fiscal
rows.read: Government finances are weighing on the euro: France now pays more than 5% to borrow for ten years, and its gap over Germany is near the widest since 2011. Moody's reviews France's credit rating on Friday, and Britain's budget follows on October 28.
rows.figure: France 10Y above 5%; OAT–Bund ~1.6–1.7pts (widest since 2011); Moody's on France Fri Oct 23; French revenue vote Oct 27; UK budget Oct 28
